slides.title: The Break Statement
slides.content: The break statement immediately exits a loop. Code after break in the same block never runs.

slides.title: The Continue Statement
slides.content: continue skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next one. The loop condition is still checked.

exercise.prompt: Choose continue to skip even numbers

slides.title: Break in Nested Loops
slides.content: A break only exits the innermost loop. To exit an outer loop, use a labeled break with goto.

exercise.prompt: The keyword to define a loop label is _____

slides.title: Continue in Nested Loops
slides.content: continue affects only the innermost loop. The outer loop continues normally.

exercise.prompt: When continue runs in nested loops, which loop continues?

slides.title: Searching with Break
slides.content: Use break to stop searching once you find what you need. This saves processing time.

exercise.prompt: Select the correct statement to exit after finding the target

slides.title: Filtering with Continue
slides.content: Use continue to skip unwanted items while processing a collection.

exercise.prompt: Use continue to skip negative values: `if (x < 0) ______;`

slides.title: Break vs Continue
slides.content: break exits the loop entirely. continue skips the current iteration and continues with the next one.

slides.title: Best Practices
slides.content: Use break when you have found what you need. Use continue to skip invalid data. Avoid overusing goto with labels.

exercise.prompt: Write a loop that prints 0-4 but stops at 3 using break
hints: Make sure your code includes the required keywords/elements: for, break, Console.WriteLine
When run, your code should output: 0, 1, 2, 3

slides.title: Flow Builder: While Loop
slides.content: Use the Flow Builder to create a while loop that counts to 2.
